_comment: Feature 26 (ORM instance loading / hydration). LOAD-DEC-01 (OWNER-DECISIONS.md
Batch 4) + LOAD-DEC-02 (Batch 5), ratified 2026-08-11.
LOAD-PY-REVALIDATE (LOAD-DEC-01, Python, the highest-value fix): hydration
(_populate) reused Field.validate() -- the SAME method save() uses -- so a
read RE-ENFORCED write-path business constraints (required/length/range/
regex/choices). A stored row that violated a constraint, or one TIGHTENED
after the row was written, raised ValueError out of cls(row) and ABORTED THE
WHOLE select() -- not just the offending row. FIXED: Field gained a new
coerce() (type coercion + JSON parse only, extracted from validate() via a
shared _coerce_type/_resolve_callable so the write path's behaviour is
byte-for-byte unchanged) and _populate now calls coerce() instead of
validate(). validate() (business constraints) stays write-path-only --
save()/ORM.validate() and AutoCrud's PUT handler are untouched. READ-ONLY
change: a bad save is still rejected (proven in the fixture).
LOAD-RUBY-ASYMMETRY + LOAD-RUBY-SIGNATURE (LOAD-DEC-01 + LOAD-DEC-02, Ruby):
Ruby had TWO hydration paths with different coercion -- from_hash (the
primary finder path) JSON-decoded json columns, but the instance load()
fed the raw driver value straight to the setter, so Model.find(id).payload
returned a parsed Hash while model.load(id).payload stayed a raw JSON
String -- the SAME row, a different type, purely by which read path was
called. FIXED: load() now hydrates via from_hash -- ONE hydration path, not
two -- and its signature is aligned to load(filter, params, include:),
matching Python's load(filter, params, include) and PHP's
load(?string $filter, array $params, ?array $include) exactly. BREAKING:
the old load(id) scalar-primary-key shortcut is REMOVED (it built the
malformed fragment "WHERE <id>", valid-but-wrong SQL that matches the
table's first row rather than raising) -- callers set the PK attribute
then call load with no args, or pass an explicit "pk = ?" filter. A
non-nil, non-String filter now raises ArgumentError naming the fix.
LOAD-NODE-SERIALIZE-OMIT (LOAD-DEC-02, Node): toDict()/toJson() SILENTLY
omitted a declared relation that was requested via `include` but never
eager-loaded (a synchronous serializer cannot lazy-load it) -- no signal at
all, so a developer who forgot `include` on the finder got a serialized
object silently missing the relation. FIXED: the omission now calls
Log.warning() naming the model, the relation, and that `include` on the
finder is needed. It still does NOT throw (serialization keeps working)
and the returned shape is UNCHANGED (the relation is still absent) --
Node-scoped, since only Node's serializer is synchronous-over-a-cache in
this way (Python/PHP/Ruby relationships are lazy descriptors that load on
access, so there is nothing to omit).
LOAD-JSON-ONLY (LOAD-DEC-02, the scalar read-coercion contract): PINNED as
JSON-only (OWNER-DECISIONS.md Batch 5 -- "pin the scalar read-coercion
contract (JSON-only today)"). Only JSON columns parse to a native object on
read; non-JSON scalars stay driver-typed in PHP/Ruby/Node (booleans hydrate
as numbers, datetimes as driver strings -- no Date/bool reconstitution) and
unchanged in Python (Python's own, separate, pre-existing scalar coercion in
fields.py -- str->datetime, int/bool normalising across driver shapes -- is
TYPE COERCION, not a business constraint, and stays intact; it is a
documented Python-specific enhancement the ledger's "pin the JSON-only
contract" does not ask the other three to adopt, and does not ask Python to
drop). No scalar-coercion code changed in any of the four frameworks.
Already-correct, reported not fixed: PHP's business-constraint overlay
($fields, read by validate()) was NEVER consulted by fill() -- LOAD-PY-
REVALIDATE never existed for PHP's OWN validation vocabulary. PHP DID have
a same-symptom bug via a different mechanism (below). Ruby's dynamic typing
and Node's erased TypeScript types mean neither language was ever at risk
of a required/length/range read-time crash -- the
constraint_violating_stored_row_still_hydrates case is a regression LOCK
for Ruby/Node, not a fix. Node's load() already delegated to selectOne()
(one hydration path) and already had the load(filter, params, include)
shape -- no LOAD-RUBY-ASYMMETRY/-SIGNATURE twin in Node.
LOAD-PHP-NONNULLABLE-HYDRATE (found during this pass, same symptom as
LOAD-PY-REVALIDATE via a different mechanism -- PHP's OWN type system, not
a re-run of the $fields overlay): the documented PHP idiom for a required
column is a NON-NULLABLE typed property (`public string $name = '';` +
$fields['name']['required']=true, see OrmValidateConstraintsTest.php).
fill()'s plain `$this->$propName = $value` THREW TypeError
("Cannot assign null to property ...$name of type string") on a stored
NULL, unhandled, aborting the whole find()/all()/select() for one row --
empirically verified against a real SQLite table with a raw NULL insert
before this pass touched the code. FIXED: fill() now catches ONLY a
null-into-non-nullable TypeError and leaves the property at its already-
initialized class default (the stored NULL cannot be literally represented
by a non-nullable property, so the class default is the closest coercion
target); any OTHER TypeError (a genuinely un-coercible non-null value)
still propagates -- that is real data corruption, not a business
constraint. #165's _assignedFields tracking moved to AFTER a successful
assignment so a skipped null-into-non-nullable set is correctly NOT
recorded as caller-touched.
Case names are shared verbatim (each language's own idiom) across the four
frameworks and gated by scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py.
NO MOCKS: real SQLite (always) + real PostgreSQL :55432 tina4/tina4 (gated --
skips cleanly when unreachable locally, a hard failure under
TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES, e.g. on the lab). Mutation-proven in all four,
2026-08-12: reinstating Python's field.validate() call in _populate turns
constraint_violating_stored_row_still_hydrates RED with the exact
"Field 'name' is required" ValueError out of hydration; reverting Ruby's
load() to the raw setattr loop turns json_column_round_trips_via_load RED
("expected a native Hash, got String"); reverting PHP's fill() try/catch
turns the same constraint case RED with the exact TypeError
("Cannot assign null to property LoadContractItemV2::$name of type
string"); reverting Node's toDict() warning turns
unloaded_relation_serialization_warns_not_silent RED (no warning text
captured). All four restored to green after each proof.
Maintainability: Python's read path is SIMPLER (coerce() has no constraint
branches at all vs validate()'s five); Ruby COLLAPSED to one hydration path
(the from_hash-duplicating setter loop in load() deleted, ~15 lines -> a
single from_hash() call + a field-copy loop). Zero new runtime deps in any
of the four.
feature: LOAD-DEC-01 / LOAD-DEC-02 - ORM instance loading / hydration

invariants.rule: A JSON column hydrates to a native object (dict/array/Hash) through every FINDER path (find/findById/all/where/select/selectOne), never a raw JSON string.
invariants.why: The baseline JSON-parse-on-read contract every finder must uphold -- the positive control that json_column_round_trips_via_load (below) is compared against.

invariants.rule: The SAME JSON column hydrates to a native object through the instance load() path too -- load() must coerce IDENTICALLY to the finder path, not leave a JSON column as a raw string.
invariants.why: Catches LOAD-RUBY-ASYMMETRY directly: pre-fix, Ruby's load() fed the raw driver value to the setter (from_hash was the only JSON-decoding path), so the SAME row read via load() vs find() returned two different types for the same column. Mutation-proven: reverting Ruby's load() to the raw setattr loop turns this case RED.

invariants.rule: A stored row that violates a constraint TIGHTENED after the row was written (a `required` field storing NULL, read through a model version that now declares it required) STILL hydrates through a finder -- it does NOT raise and does NOT abort a page of results. The SAME model's write path (save()) still REJECTS a new row missing the required field -- this is a read-only fix, not a deleted constraint.
invariants.why: Catches LOAD-PY-REVALIDATE: pre-fix, Python's _populate reused Field.validate(), so a required-but-NULL stored row raised ValueError out of cls(row) and aborted the WHOLE select(), not just the offending row -- tightening a constraint could make existing data unreadable. Also catches LOAD-PHP-NONNULLABLE-HYDRATE, found during this pass: PHP's documented required-field idiom is a non-nullable typed property, and fill()'s plain assignment threw an unhandled TypeError on a stored NULL, aborting find()/all() the same way, via PHP's own type system rather than a re-run of $fields. Ruby's dynamic typing and Node's erased types mean this is a regression LOCK for those two, not a fix. Mutation-proven: reinstating Python's field.validate() call reproduces the exact 'Field name is required' ValueError; reverting PHP's fill() try/catch reproduces the exact 'Cannot assign null to property ...$name of type string' TypeError. Both restored green after the proof.

invariants.rule: A SELECT naming only some columns yields an instance with the selected fields set from the row and every OTHER declared field at its class default -- never a crash, never a stale/wrong value.
invariants.why: A pre-existing behaviour (every hydration path only assigns keys present in the row) this fixture locks in as a permanent regression guard alongside the LOAD-DEC-01/02 fixes, so a future change to any hydration path cannot quietly break partial-select support.

invariants.rule: Node-scoped (Python/PHP/Ruby relationships are lazy descriptors with nothing to omit): toDict()/toJson() requesting a relation via `include` that was never eager-loaded still OMITS it from the result (the shape does not change -- a synchronous serializer cannot lazy-load), but now calls Log.warning() naming the model, the relation, and that `include` on the finder is needed. It never throws.
invariants.why: Pre-fix the omission was completely silent -- a developer who forgot `include` on the finder that produced the instance got a serialized object silently missing the relation, with no signal at all (the warning that DOES exist today only fires for an unrecognised include name, a different code path). Mutation-proven: reverting the warning call turns unloaded_relation_serialization_warns_not_silent RED (no warning text captured in the same run that still shows the relation correctly omitted).
